To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) females of the Trinidadian guppy, Poecilia reticulata, preferentially produce offspring with males who are genetically unrelated; (2) sperm from unrelated males are more competitive than that from related males in sperm competition; and (3) ovarian fluid from females reduces the swimming velocity of sperm from related males.

(i) female guppies prefer to mate with unrelated males, (ii) this preference can be mediated by post-copulatory processes and (iii) the OF of females may be involved in the mediation of this preference.
cryptic female preference for unrelated mates can be mediated by post-copulatory sperm competition bias.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms underlying female choice for unrelated males, and the results are important for our understanding of the evolution of polyandry.
the evolution of polyandry in the guppy and the possible role played by sperm competition in this process.
the evolutionary consequences of mating with relatives.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of this study provide evidence that the OF from females can mediate cryptic female choice in favor of unrelated males, thus reducing the costs of inbreeding in polyandrous guppies.
the results of this work provide the first experimental evidence that cryptic female choice for unrelated males can occur in the guppy.
the OF of a female is able to bias paternity in favour of genetically unrelated males.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
polyandry can evolve in females as a mechanism of inbreeding avoidance.
cryptic female choice in the guppy may be driven by the ability of females to bias paternity in favour of unrelated males, through the production of OF that affects sperm performance in competition.
the sperm of genetically unrelated males have a higher chance of fertilizing an egg than those of a full-sib male.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sperm competition is not only a male-driven process.
the cost of mating inbreeders is not only limited to the pre-copulatory phase but also extends to the post-copulatory phase.
cryptic female choice is a powerful post-copulatory mechanism that can bias paternity towards genetically nonrelated males.
